debug_rounds.title: Cart totals drift and old state changes
debug_rounds.scenario: SHOP-2231: The storefront shows a total of $0.30000000000000004 for a cart with a $0.10 sample and a $0.20 sample. Separately, the 'undo add to cart' feature in the React app is broken: after adding a second unit of an item, the previous state object also shows quantity 2, so the UI never re-renders correctly.
hints: There are two unrelated problems: one is about numbers, one is about object identity. Check the 'existing' branch of `add` first.
`existing.qty += qty` changes an object that the previous state still points at. Separately, summing decimal dollar amounts with `+` cannot be exact in binary floating point.

Replace the matching line with a copy (`map` + spread) instead of editing it. For money, convert each price to integer cents, do all arithmetic on integers (round the discount once), and divide by 100 at the very end.
debug_rounds.explanation: Bug 1 is state mutation: the reducer copied the items array but not the line item inside it, so the old state shared the object that was edited; immutable updates must copy every level that changes. Bug 2 is floating point money: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in IEEE-754. Do money maths in integer cents and round once at the discount step.

debug_rounds.title: Last page is empty and page count is wrong
debug_rounds.scenario: ADMIN-884: In the users table, page 1 skips the first ten users and the 'Next' button disappears one page too early. With 25 users and 10 per page the footer says there are 2 pages. Pages are 1-based in the UI.
hints: Only `paginate.js` is wrong; `labels.js` already assumes 1-based pages. Compare how `describeRange` computes the first item with how `paginate` computes `start`.
`start` treats `page` as 0-based, and `Math.floor` drops the final partial page.
Use `(page - 1) * perPage` for the offset and `Math.ceil` for the page count.
debug_rounds.explanation: Two classic pagination errors: a 0-based offset formula applied to 1-based page numbers (page 1 skipped the first page of data), and floor instead of ceil when dividing item count by page size (the partial last page was not counted, so hasNext was false too early).

debug_rounds.title: Query strings lose zeros and break on special characters
debug_rounds.scenario: API-1517: The search client builds URLs with our small query helper. Searching for 'R&D budget' returns results for 'R' only, and filters like 'page=0' or 'archived=false' are silently dropped, so the backend applies its defaults instead.
hints: Two separate lines in `buildQuery` are at fault. One decides which values are skipped, the other builds the pair string.
`if (!value)` is true for `0`, `false` and `""`, which are all legitimate values. And values are concatenated raw, so `&` and `=` inside them corrupt the structure.
Skip only `null`/`undefined`, and wrap both key and value in `encodeURIComponent`.
debug_rounds.explanation: Truthiness checks conflate 'missing' with 'falsy but meaningful'; only null and undefined mean absent. And URL components must be percent-encoded, otherwise user data can terminate a parameter early (a mini injection bug).

debug_rounds.title: Validator rejects zero and accepts NaN
debug_rounds.scenario: FORM-310: In the order form, entering a quantity of 0 for a free sample shows 'qty is required' even though 0 is allowed. Meanwhile, someone pasted 'abc' into the age field, the UI parsed it to NaN, and the form happily submitted it because 'min 18' did not complain.
hints: Look at `isEmpty` for the zero problem, and at what every comparison with NaN evaluates to for the NaN problem.
Loose equality: `0 == ""` and `false == ""` are both true. And `NaN < 18` and `NaN > 65` are both false, so a rule written as 'fail when out of range' lets NaN through.
Use strict comparisons in `isEmpty`. Write min/max as 'pass when the condition holds' (`v >= n`) so that NaN, which fails every comparison, produces an error.
debug_rounds.explanation: `==` coerces types, so 0 and false compare equal to the empty string. NaN is never less than or greater than anything, so negative-form range checks (`v < n` means error) accept it. Positive-form checks fail safe.

debug_rounds.title: Leaderboard order is scrambled and ties are ranked wrong
debug_rounds.scenario: GAME-77: The weekly leaderboard sometimes lists a lower score above a higher one. Players tied on points should share a rank (1, 2, 2, 4) but get 1, 2, 3, 4. Also, the 'players' array on the profile page changes order after the leaderboard renders.
hints: Three problems in `rank`: what the comparator returns, what the sort touches, and how the rank number is assigned.
A sort comparator must return a negative, zero or positive number. A boolean becomes 1 or 0 and never says 'comes first'. Also `Array.prototype.sort` sorts in place.
Sort a copy with `b.score - a.score` (then name as tie-break). Track the previous score and previous rank; if the score equals the previous one reuse its rank, otherwise use `i + 1`.
debug_rounds.explanation: A boolean comparator is a classic JS trap: it never returns a negative value, so engines cannot order elements correctly. `sort` mutates the original array, which leaked ordering changes elsewhere. And `index + 1` ignores ties; competition ranking reuses the previous rank on equal scores.

debug_rounds.title: Search box fires too often and loses its context
debug_rounds.scenario: UI-902: The autocomplete box is supposed to wait until the user stops typing for 300 ms, but it fires one request for every keystroke once the delay passes. Method handlers wrapped with our debounce see 'this' as undefined. And the scroll-tracking throttle ignores the very first event of a session and also swallows an event that arrives exactly one interval after the previous one.
hints: Three bugs across two files: debounce has two (look at what happens to earlier timers and to the receiver), throttle has one root cause pair in its initial state and comparison.

A debounced function must cancel the previously scheduled call each time. An arrow callback calling `fn(...args)` drops `this`. In throttle, `last = 0` means 'a call happened at time 0', and `>` excludes the boundary.
In debounce: `clearTimeout(timer)` before scheduling, capture `this` in `const ctx = this`, and call `fn.apply(ctx, args)`. In throttle: start with `last = -Infinity` and compare with `>=`.
debug_rounds.explanation: Debounce without clearing the previous timer is just a delayed call per event. `this` is dynamic in JS, so a wrapper must capture it from the call site (`function`, not arrow) and forward it with `apply`. Throttle's initial 'last call' time must be 'never' (-Infinity), and the boundary is inclusive when the interval has fully elapsed.

debug_rounds.title: Promise pool returns results out of order and over-runs its limit
debug_rounds.scenario: INFRA-455: The thumbnail uploader uses pool(tasks, 4) so we do not hammer the storage API. Monitoring shows 5 simultaneous uploads, and the returned URL list does not line up with the input files: the fastest uploads come first, so the UI attaches thumbnails to the wrong images.
hints: Look at the worker loop bound and at where each result is stored.
`i <= limit` starts limit + 1 workers. And `results.push` records results in the order tasks finish, not the order they were given.
Loop `i < limit`, and capture `const index = next++` so you can write `results[index] = ...`.
debug_rounds.explanation: An inclusive loop bound created one extra worker, breaking the concurrency guarantee. Pushing results by completion order is a race-dependent bug: parallel async work must write each result into its own slot using the task's index.

debug_rounds.title: Retry helper never retries and backs off linearly
debug_rounds.scenario: PAY-1204: During yesterday's gateway blip, our retry(fn, { retries: 3 }) wrapper gave up on the first error without a single retry. When we looked closer, even if it had retried, it would have made only 3 attempts in total instead of 1 + 3, and the delays were 0, 200, 400 instead of an exponential 100, 200, 400.
hints: Three independent defects, all inside `retry.js`: one about async control flow, one about how many times the loop runs, one about the delay formula.
`return fn(attempt)` inside `try` returns the promise without awaiting it, so a rejection happens after the `try` block has already exited. Also, `retries` means retries, not total attempts.
Use `return await fn(attempt)`, loop `attempt <= retries`, rethrow on the last attempt before sleeping, and sleep `baseMs * 2 ** attempt`.
debug_rounds.explanation: A `try/catch` only catches rejections of promises that are awaited inside it; `return promise` skips the catch. The loop bound confused 'retries' with 'attempts', and a linear formula with a zero first term gave no initial delay. Sleeping after the final failure is also pointless and was removed.

debug_rounds.title: TTL cache serves expired and drops falsy values
debug_rounds.scenario: CACHE-63: Feature flags are cached for 60 seconds. Operators report that cache.has('beta') still says true long after expiry, an entry is still served at exactly the 60 s mark, and a flag whose value is legitimately 0 is re-fetched from the database on every request because the cache seems to ignore it.
hints: Check three places: the expiry comparison, `has`, and the 'is it cached?' test in `getOrSet`.
`<` leaves an entry alive at the exact moment it expires; `has` never looks at the expiry time; `if (hit)` is a truthiness check, so `0`, `false` and `""` look like a miss.
Use `<=` in `_expired`, make `has` go through the same liveness check as `get`, and in `getOrSet` ask `has(key)` instead of testing the value.
debug_rounds.explanation: Three expiry-related slips: an inclusive/exclusive boundary, a second read path (`has`) that bypassed the expiry logic, and truthiness used to detect a cache hit. Any read path must share one 'is this entry live?' helper, and 'hit' must be determined by presence, not by value.

debug_rounds.title: Event emitter skips listeners and crashes on odd event names
debug_rounds.scenario: PLAT-318: In the plugin host, a one-shot 'ready' listener sometimes causes the next listener on the same event to be silently skipped. Calling the unsubscribe function twice removed somebody else's handler. And a plugin that emits an event called 'constructor' crashes the whole host with a TypeError.
hints: Three separate flaws in `emitter.js`: how `off` locates the handler, how `emit` loops, and what data structure holds the handlers.

`indexOf` returns -1 when nothing matches and `splice(-1, 1)` removes the LAST element. A `for...of` over an array that a listener mutates (the `once` wrapper removes itself) shifts the remaining items. A plain `{}` already has keys like `constructor`.
Guard `off` with `if (i !== -1)`, iterate over a copy (`[...list]`) in `emit`, and store handlers in a `Map`.
debug_rounds.explanation: Negative index in `splice` is a classic: `indexOf` failing returns -1 which splice interprets as 'from the end'. Mutating a collection while iterating it skips elements; snapshot before dispatch. Using a plain object as a dictionary with user-controlled keys collides with inherited properties; use `Map` (or a null-prototype object).

debug_rounds.title: Invoices are off by a cent and negative amounts print garbage
debug_rounds.scenario: BILL-2090: Finance reports invoices where a $19.99 item shows up as $19.98. Refunds are displayed as '-$-2.-50' instead of '-$1.50'. And when a $100.00 dinner is split three ways, the three shares add up to $99.99, so someone is always short a cent.
hints: All three bugs live in `money.js`; `invoice.js` is a consumer. Print `19.99 * 100` in a REPL to see the first.
`parseInt` truncates, and `19.99 * 100` is `1998.9999999999998`. Negative numbers: `Math.floor(-150 / 100)` is -2 and `-150 % 100` is -50. The even split throws away `total % parts`.
Use `Math.round`, format `Math.abs(cents)` and add the sign separately, and hand the remainder out one cent at a time to the first `remainder` parts.
debug_rounds.explanation: Money bugs come from three places: converting decimals to integers (truncating a value that is 1 ulp below the true amount), sign handling when splitting into dollars and cents with floor/modulo on negatives, and integer division that loses the remainder. The invariant for splits is that shares sum exactly to the total.

debug_rounds.title: Undo restores the wrong state and redo never clears
debug_rounds.scenario: APP-1120: In the todo app, toggling a task and pressing undo leaves it checked. After undoing an add and then adding something new, 'redo' brings back the old item on top of the new state. Clicking 'complete' on an item that was just deleted in another tab throws, and leaves a phantom entry in the undo history.
hints: The three symptoms map to three code paths: the snapshot helper, the place where history is recorded, and the order of validation vs. recording.

`slice()` copies the array but not the todo objects inside it, so `toggle` mutates objects that old snapshots still reference. Nothing ever empties `future`. And `_snapshot()` runs before checking that the id exists.
Snapshot with `map((t) => ({ ...t }))`, reset `future = []` whenever you record a new snapshot, and look up the todo (return `false` if missing) before committing.
debug_rounds.explanation: Undo/redo needs deep-enough snapshots (shallow copies share nested objects), a redo stack that is invalidated by any new edit (otherwise history branches into nonsense), and history entries must only be recorded for operations that actually change state.

debug_rounds.title: Middleware chain: errors escape and timings read zero
debug_rounds.scenario: API-3011: After we moved to our in-house Koa-style middleware runner, the error boundary no longer catches errors thrown in async route handlers (requests crash with unhandled rejections), response-time headers always say 0 ms, and a buggy auth middleware that calls next() twice runs the handler twice (double charges!) instead of failing loudly.
hints: The three symptoms are in two files. Two of them share the same root cause: a promise-returning call that is not awaited. The third is a guard in `compose.js`.

`return next()` inside `try` hands back the promise before it settles, so `catch` never sees a rejection; `next();` with no `await` lets the timer read the clock before downstream finishes. In `compose`, think about what `i` equals the second time the same `next()` is invoked.
Use `return await next()` in `errorBoundary`, `await next()` in `timing`, and make the guard `i <= index`.
debug_rounds.explanation: This is the Koa `compose` contract. A `try/catch` only handles errors from awaited promises; un-awaited `next()` makes later code run too early. And the double-call guard must be inclusive: the second call to the same `next` dispatches the same index, which is equal (not less than) to the recorded one.

debug_rounds.title: Billing dates drift to the 29th and mutate subscriptions
debug_rounds.scenario: BILL-3312: A customer who subscribed on Jan 31 is billed on Jan 31, Mar 2, Apr 2 and then the 2nd of each month forever. After we fixed that locally, the next invoice dates were Jan 31, Feb 29, Mar 29, Apr 29, so they permanently lose days. Also the 'trial ends' preview moves the subscription's start date.
hints: Find three defects: one function that changes its argument, one that mishandles month lengths, and one loop that compounds error.
`setUTCMonth` on Jan 31 asks for 'Feb 31', which JavaScript normalises to Mar 2 (or 3). `addDays` edits the date it is given. `billingDates` feeds each rounded result into the next addition.

Copy the date in `addDays`; in `addMonths` set the day to 1 first, move the month, then set the day to `min(originalDay, daysInTargetMonth)`; in `billingDates` always add `i` months to the original `start`.
debug_rounds.explanation: Date arithmetic traps: Date objects are mutable; month overflow is silently normalised instead of clamped; and iterating 'add one month to the previous result' accumulates clamping losses, so you must compute every occurrence from the anchor date.

debug_rounds.title: Config merge corrupts defaults and crashes on null
debug_rounds.scenario: CFG-872: Our service builds its config with resolveConfig(overrides). After one tenant overrides the database port, every later tenant in the same process also gets that port, because the shared defaults changed. A tenant that sets 'cache: null' to disable caching crashes the loader with a TypeError, and a tenant's 'allowedHosts' list is merged index-by-index with the default list instead of replacing it. Security also flagged that merging untrusted JSON can modify Object.prototype.
hints: `merge.js` is the only file that needs changing. There are three separate problems: the 'is it an object?' test, who owns the result object, and which keys you are willing to copy.

`typeof null === 'object'` and `typeof [] === 'object'`. Also, `target[key] = src[key]` stores a reference, so later merges write through into the source. And `JSON.parse` can create an own key literally named `__proto__`.

Make the merge build a fresh result (deep-cloning values it copies), treat only non-null non-array objects as mergeable, replace arrays wholesale, and skip `__proto__` / `constructor` / `prototype` keys.
debug_rounds.explanation: Three classic merge bugs: `typeof` is not a plain-object check (null and arrays); copying by reference means the result aliases inputs, so mutating a 'copy' mutates the defaults; and recursively merging into attacker-supplied keys like `__proto__` is prototype pollution (CVE-class issue in several popular libraries).

debug_rounds.title: JSON diff crashes on null and reports phantom changes
debug_rounds.scenario: AUDIT-540: The audit log diffs old and new records. It throws 'Cannot use in operator' when a field goes from null to an object, reports NaN to NaN as a change on every save of records with an empty numeric field, and says 'toString' was modified rather than added when a customer adds a custom field with that name.
hints: All three bugs are in `diff.js` and each is a one-line misconception about a JavaScript primitive: `typeof`, `===`, and `in`.
`typeof null` is `'object'`, so null is treated as a container. `NaN === NaN` is false. And `'toString' in {}` is true because `in` also walks the prototype chain.

Define `isObj` as `v !== null && typeof v === 'object'`, compare scalars with a helper that also treats two NaNs as equal (not `Object.is`, which would split 0 and -0), and use `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call` instead of `in`.
debug_rounds.explanation: `typeof null === 'object'` is the oldest wart in the language; `NaN` is the only value not equal to itself, so equality checks on data that can hold NaN need a special case; and the `in` operator includes inherited properties, so for data-as-dictionary code you want an own-property check.

debug_rounds.title: Rate limiter starves clients and lets bursts through
debug_rounds.scenario: EDGE-2207: Support says a client polling every 400 ms against a 1 request/second limit is blocked forever even though it is well within its quota. Meanwhile a cron client that was idle all night fires 50 requests at 9:00 and gets all of them through, and the Retry-After header we return says '1' for clients that must wait 2.5 seconds.
hints: All three defects are in `_bucket` and `retryAfterMs` in `bucket.js`. Think about what the refill line does to a fraction of a token, what stops it growing, and what unit `retryAfterMs` returns.

`Math.floor` on every refill throws away partial progress, but `last` is still moved forward, so a client polling faster than one token interval never accrues anything. Nothing caps `tokens` at `capacity`. `(cost - tokens) / refillPerSec` is seconds, not milliseconds.
Keep tokens fractional, clamp with `Math.min(this.capacity, ...)`, and multiply the wait by 1000 before `Math.ceil`.
debug_rounds.explanation: Token-bucket correctness rests on three invariants: tokens are continuous (don't round on refill, or frequent callers lose progress), tokens never exceed capacity (otherwise idle clients accumulate unlimited bursts), and units are consistent (seconds vs. milliseconds in the retry hint).

debug_rounds.title: Batch loader fetches duplicates and mishandles per-key errors
debug_rounds.scenario: GQL-6401: Our GraphQL resolvers use a DataLoader-style BatchLoader to avoid N+1 queries. After a refactor, requests for the same user in one tick produce duplicate IDs in the batched SQL ('WHERE id IN (7,7,8)'), loadMany(ids) throws 'Cannot read properties of undefined', and when one user in a batch is missing, the resolver receives an Error object as if it were a user and renders 'undefined' fields instead of failing that one field.
hints: Three separate faults in `loader.js`: how in-flight lookups are remembered, how `loadMany` calls `load`, and what happens to Error entries returned by `batchFn`.

The cache is only filled after the batch returns, so a second `load(7)` in the same tick finds nothing and queues a duplicate. `keys.map(this.load)` passes an unbound method. The documented contract says an Error entry rejects only its own key, but the code resolves with it.

Cache the promise itself immediately in `load` (so duplicates share it), call `keys.map((k) => this.load(k))`, and reject jobs whose value is an `Error`. Because you now cache promises, remember to evict a key from the cache whenever its promise rejects, otherwise one failure is cached forever.
debug_rounds.explanation: This is the DataLoader design: memoize the in-flight promise rather than the value so same-tick duplicates collapse; keep `this` bound when passing methods as callbacks; and honour the per-key error contract. A promise cache introduces one more obligation: rejected entries must be evicted so transient errors are retryable.
